basic_info.name: Mario Klingemann (Quasimondo)
basic_info.active_years: 2015-present (generative/AI art; earlier digital art from ~2000s; net art from ~1998)

practice_description.medium: GAN-generated imagery, neural network art, generative installation, creative coding, real-time AI systems
practice_description.practice_summary: Mario Klingemann is a pioneer of GAN-based art who treats the navigation of neural network latent spaces as a primary artistic practice — exploring the boundaries, glitches, and uncanny territories of machine-generated imagery with a focus on human perception, portraiture, and the aesthetic possibilities of algorithmic systems.
practice_description.methodology: Klingemann works through intensive, iterative experimentation with neural network architectures — modifying GANs, training on custom datasets, and exploring the full topology of latent spaces including edge cases, failure modes, and interpolation artefacts that reveal the inner logic of the models. His methodology is distinctively exploratory and prolific: rapid prototyping, sharing work-in-progress on social media (Twitter/X), and treating the latent space as a vast territory to be mapped through intuition and systematic navigation. He often works with found and historical imagery (archival photographs, art history datasets, medical imagery) to create haunting, dreamlike outputs. He has built custom tools for real-time latent space exploration and developed techniques for controlling and steering GAN outputs. Recently Google Arts & Culture Artist in Residence.

relevance_to_sense_room.relevance_summary: Klingemann's practice defines what it means to navigate latent space as artistic practice — he has mapped more territory in GAN embedding spaces than perhaps any other artist. His work demonstrates how the space between trained images contains its own aesthetic logic and can be traversed as a genuinely new medium, directly relevant to how A(DAI)'s knowledge graph could become navigable experiential terrain.
relevance_to_sense_room.art_as_substrate: Partially. Klingemann's generative outputs — continuous streams of morphing GAN imagery — can function as visual substrates, especially in installation contexts. However, much of his work is oriented toward discrete images or short video loops shared online rather than ambient environmental substrates.
relevance_to_sense_room.relational_composition: Partially. The latent space itself encodes relationships between all images in the training set — navigating it reveals how the model represents connections between visual concepts. Klingemann's interpolation works trace paths between visual states, making these latent relationships visible. However, the composition is navigational rather than explicitly graph-based.
relevance_to_sense_room.self_recomposing: Yes, in installation works. Klingemann has created real-time generative installations that continuously traverse latent space, producing endlessly evolving imagery. The real-time systems respond to parameters that can be modulated. Autonomous generative works run indefinitely without repeating.

works.title: Memories of Passersby I
works.description: An autonomous AI artwork consisting of two screens displaying continuously generated GAN portraits — an endless procession of faces that exist only briefly before dissolving into the next. The system runs on a custom-built computer, generating unique portraits in real-time forever. One of the first AI artworks sold at auction (Sotheby's, 2019). The portraits emerge from and dissolve back into abstract forms, visualising the latent space traversal.
works.relevance: Demonstrates autonomous, endlessly generating AI art — a self-sustaining generative system that produces unique visual output indefinitely. A model for how A(DAI)'s Sense Room could feature continuously generating, never-repeating visual content driven by underlying intelligence.

works.title: Neural Glitch / Neurographic Portraits
works.description: A body of work exploring the glitches, artefacts, and edge cases of GAN-generated portraiture. Rather than pursuing photorealistic generation, Klingemann deliberately seeks out the uncanny, distorted, and dreamlike states that emerge at the boundaries of what the model has learned — faces merging, features dissolving, impossible anatomies.
works.relevance: Demonstrates artistic practice at the edges of latent space — where the model's learned representations break down and produce something genuinely new. Relevant to A(DAI)'s interest in what emerges at the boundaries and intersections of knowledge domains.

works.title: Appropriate Response
works.description: A real-time interactive installation where a camera captures visitors and a neural network responds by generating AI imagery that 'responds' to the visitor's appearance, expression, and posture. The system creates a visual dialogue between human and machine perception.
works.relevance: Interactive AI system that creates a feedback loop between human presence and machine generation — visitors see themselves reflected through the distorting mirror of a neural network. Relevant to Sense Room concepts of responsive, presence-aware environments.

protocol_art_resonance.protocol_art_summary: Klingemann treats the exploration of neural network architectures, training procedures, and latent space navigation techniques as artistic practice. He has developed and shared novel methods for controlling GAN outputs, steering generation, and navigating latent spaces. His prolific sharing of techniques and discoveries on social media functions as a form of open protocol-sharing for the AI art community.
protocol_art_resonance.system_designed: Custom tools for real-time latent space navigation and GAN output control. Autonomous generative systems (Memories of Passersby I) that function as self-sustaining art machines. Various techniques for GAN training, interpolation, and output steering shared through social media and talks.

commons_orientation.commons_summary: Klingemann is notably generous in sharing techniques, discoveries, and work-in-progress through social media (Twitter/X), making his practice unusually transparent. He has shared code snippets, training techniques, and conceptual approaches openly. However, finished artworks are sold through commercial galleries and auctions (Sotheby's, Onkaos gallery). The practice combines radical openness in process with commercial enclosure of final outputs. Some code shared on GitHub but no systematic open-source release of tools.

governance_model.governance_detail: Klingemann works as an independent solo artist. Creative decisions are entirely his own. Institutional residencies (Google Arts & Culture) provide resources but not creative direction. No collective governance structure.

consent_and_authorship.consent_approach: Training data includes historical photographs, art history images, and found imagery — often archival material where consent from depicted individuals is not obtainable. Interactive works capture visitor imagery in real-time for neural network processing but do not store it. The ethics of training on historical imagery (especially portraiture) is not always explicitly addressed.
consent_and_authorship.authorship_model: Solo authorship attributed to Klingemann. Machine co-authorship is an implicit dimension — the GAN generates the imagery — but Klingemann positions himself firmly as the artist who designs the system, curates the training data, navigates the latent space, and selects the outputs. The machine is a medium, not a co-author, in his framing.

liveness_and_duration.temporal_detail: Autonomous works like Memories of Passersby I generate continuously and indefinitely — the system traverses latent space in real-time, producing unique outputs that never repeat. Interactive installations respond to visitor presence in real-time. The generation is live, not pre-rendered, with the underlying neural network producing new outputs at each moment.

data_materiality.data_sources: Historical portrait photography, art history image collections, medical/anatomical imagery, archival photographs, found imagery, curated image datasets specific to each project. The choice of training data is a primary artistic decision — what the model learns to see defines what it can generate.
data_materiality.data_provenance: Mixed. Training data includes historical/archival imagery (often out of copyright or of unclear copyright status), publicly available art reproductions, web-sourced images, and curated collections. The provenance and consent status of training data is not always explicitly documented — a common characteristic of early GAN art practice.

embedding_space_relevance.embedding_summary: Absolutely central. Klingemann is one of the defining practitioners of latent space navigation as artistic practice. His work is fundamentally about exploring the topology of GAN embedding spaces — finding interesting regions, tracing paths between states, discovering what emerges at boundaries and interpolations. He has developed an intuitive fluency with high-dimensional spaces that few other artists match, treating latent space as a territory to be explored with the same curiosity and intentionality as a painter approaches a canvas.
embedding_space_relevance.multimodal: Primarily visual. Klingemann's work is overwhelmingly image-based, focused on GAN-generated imagery. Some installation works include sound design, but the practice does not typically span multiple modalities in a unified embedding framework.

exhibition_modality.spatial_description: Works manifest as autonomous screen-based installations (Memories of Passersby I as a bespoke two-screen furniture object), interactive camera-based installations, large-scale prints, online/social media (extensive Twitter presence sharing generated imagery), and NFTs. The autonomous installations are designed as self-contained objects that generate endlessly. Gallery presentations range from single screens to room-scale installations.

interoperability.composability: The generative systems produce continuous visual output streams that could theoretically serve as inputs to other systems. However, installations like Memories of Passersby I are designed as self-contained autonomous objects. No APIs or standard interfaces are exposed for external integration.
interoperability.technical_openness: Partially open. Techniques and code snippets are shared through social media and talks. Some code on GitHub. But complete systems and trained models are not formally open-sourced. The practice is transparent about methods but does not systematically release reusable tools.

technical_approach.stack: Python, PyTorch/TensorFlow for GAN training, StyleGAN/StyleGAN2, BigGAN, custom GAN architectures, NVIDIA GPUs for training and real-time inference, custom real-time rendering systems for autonomous installations, RunwayML (early adopter), Google Colab for experimentation, various GAN interpolation and steering techniques.

network_position.scene_affiliation: AI art, GAN art, generative art, creative coding, NFT art. One of the most visible and influential figures in the early GAN art movement (2017-2020). Connected to Google Arts & Culture (artist in residence), the commercial AI art market (Sotheby's, galleries), the crypto/NFT art ecosystem, and the broader creative coding community. Active social media presence makes him a node for sharing techniques and discoveries.
network_position.connections: Memo Akten (both early GAN/neural network art pioneers, share techniques and conceptual territory). Refik Anadol (both create AI-generated visuals, but Klingemann works at a more intimate, experimental scale). Sofia Crespo (both GAN art practitioners, shared generative art community, but different subject matter — Klingemann focuses on human perception/portraiture, Crespo on biology/ecology). Holly Herndon / Mat Dryhurst (connected through AI art community discussions around authorship and consent).

potential_role_in_adai.role_detail: Klingemann's practice provides the most extensive body of work demonstrating latent space navigation as artistic practice. He offers: (1) a deep practical vocabulary for what it means to navigate high-dimensional spaces artistically, (2) examples of autonomous generative systems that run indefinitely — relevant to Sense Room infrastructure, (3) a model for how process transparency (sharing techniques publicly) can coexist with commercial art practice, (4) understanding of the aesthetic properties of latent space — its topology, boundaries, and emergent qualities. His work is essential reference for understanding what AI-driven visual generation can look and feel like.
